claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The relatively low hardness and strength are governed by inherently high stacking-fault energy.
The relatively low hardness and strength are governed by minimal lattice distortion.
High stacking-fault energy and minimal lattice distortion facilitate dislocation mobility.
Greater dislocation mobility produces favorable ductility and machinability.
Insufficient dislocation pinning results in lower hardness and strength.
The starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a single-phase, simple solid-solution microstructure.
Increasing Ti content will enhance local lattice distortion.
A suitable heat treatment can induce chemical short-range ordering.
Nearly balanced atomic sizes and interactions in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produce only modest lattice distortion.
Modest lattice distortion leads to higher stacking-fault energy and limited dislocation pinning.
Increasing compositional imbalance increases lattice distortion.
Increasing compositional imbalance locally lowers stacking-fault energy.
Greater compositional imbalance improves dislocation pinning and thereby increases hardening and strength.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have higher dislocation mobility than a compositionally modified, higher-distortion variant.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have a lower work-hardening rate than the modified variant.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have lower hardness and yield strength than the modified variant.
The equimolar alloy will exhibit fewer dislocation obstacles and lower dislocation-density accumulation than the modified variant.
